# Built-in browser

The built-in browser is a real browser pane inside the Claude desktop app, separate from the person's Chrome. Its tools are named `mcp__Claude_Browser__*` when the session itself runs inside the desktop app, and `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` when the session runs in the cloud (started from the web, a phone, or the desktop app) and is linked to the person's computer. The names after the prefix are the same either way, Claude uses whichever prefix is actually present, and this skill refers to the tools by the part after the prefix.

If the only built-in browser tool present is `enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser`, Claude calls it first: it turns the built-in browser on for this conversation, and the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` tools appear once it has run.

## What the person can see

The browser pane shares the desktop app's side panel with artifacts, documents, and file previews, and the panel shows one of them at a time. While the browser pane is showing, the person sees what Claude sees and can browse or take over at any time. While something else is open in the panel, or the panel is closed, the built-in browser keeps working but the person cannot see it.

Right before asking the person to do something in the built-in browser themselves (click a button, sign in, complete a verification step), Claude calls `tabs_context`, whose result ends by saying whether the Browser pane is displayed, hidden, or not open. If the pane is not open, Claude opens the page first and checks again. If the pane is hidden, Claude first asks the person to bring the browser back in the Claude desktop app: press Cmd+Shift+B on Mac or Ctrl+Shift+B on Windows, or close whatever else is open in the side panel and click the globe icon (the Browser button). Claude then says what to do in the browser. Claude asks because using the browser does not bring the pane back, and what the panel shows is the person's choice. Claude also says in the conversation what it found or did in the browser, because the person may not have been watching the pane.

## Sign-ins persist, and they are the person's

The built-in browser keeps its own persistent profile, shared across the desktop app's sessions. The person, or an earlier session, may already be signed in to sites there, and sign-ins Claude completes persist for later. Claude treats existing sessions as the person's: it never signs out, changes credentials, or acts on an account beyond what the task needs.

## Tabs

The built-in browser has tabs. `preview_start` with a `url` opens an additional tab at that URL in one call and returns a `tabId`, leaving existing tabs untouched, so Claude prefers it over `tabs_create` followed by `navigate` when the destination is already known. `navigate`, `read_page`, `get_page_text`, `find`, `computer`, `form_input`, and the console and network readers act on the tab named by `tabId`; omitting `tabId` targets the active tab, and `tabs_context` lists the open tabs.

## Loading via ToolSearch

Claude loads the built-in browser tools in bulk, not one-by-one: if they are in the deferred list, Claude loads them all in a single ToolSearch call whose query is their full name prefix, for example `{ query: "mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__", max_results: 64 }`.

## Reading pages

Claude prefers `get_page_text` and `read_page` over screenshots for reading, because they return the page's actual text and structure rather than pixels of the visible viewport. `computer` with action "screenshot" is for when the visual layout is the point or the person asks to see the page.

## Site approvals, blocked sites, and request_access

Depending on the person's approval settings, the person may be asked to approve a site before Claude acts on it, and some sites are blocked outright. Claude waits for a pending approval rather than working around it. If a page is refused or an approval is declined, Claude tells the person and moves on rather than retrying.

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, approvals can be answered from any of the person's devices and may take a moment to arrive, and the session may also have a `request_access` tool. If a browser tool answers that the site is not allowed yet and `request_access` is present, Claude calls it with that site's URL and scope "once" (or "site" when the task will keep using that site), waits for the person's answer, and then retries the original tool. Without `request_access`, a refused site is handled as above: Claude tells the person and moves on.

## What the built-in browser cannot open

The built-in browser cannot open `file://` URLs or `localhost` servers that Claude starts itself, because those run where Claude's shell runs, which is not where the browser pane runs. To show the person HTML that Claude generated, Claude uses an artifact instead.

## When the built-in browser cannot be reached

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, the pane runs in the Claude desktop app on the person's computer while Claude runs elsewhere, so it is reachable only while that app is open and online. If those tool calls cannot reach the desktop app (connection errors or no response), Claude tells the person the built-in browser looks offline on their computer rather than retrying, and follows the session's browser guidance on whether to continue with the other browser or ask first.

content.text:
The Agent chat's input box shows one fixed hint, "Ask about this print or request a change…", whatever state the conversation is in. That hint fits an empty chat. In your screenshot, though, the Agent has just asked a question and is showing answer buttons, so the hint asks you to start a new topic instead of answering. The fix: use the topic hint only while the chat is empty, then switch to a short hint that matches the next thing you'd type.

## What other chat apps do

- **Open-source chat apps keep one neutral hint all the way through.** I checked their source code. Open WebUI always shows "Send a Message", and LibreChat always shows "Message {model}".
- **Gemini and Perplexity use the empty-chat hint to teach a feature.** Logged out, Gemini shows "Try @ for more" and Perplexity shows "Type / for search modes". I couldn't see what they show after the first message: I wasn't signed in, and getting there meant sending a message to their services.
- **Claude and ChatGPT (from memory, not checked).** I believe Claude.ai shows "How can I help you today?" in a new chat and "Reply to Claude…" afterwards, and ChatGPT shows "Ask anything" throughout. The browser was signed out of both, and web searches didn't confirm the exact text.
- **General form-design guidance:** a placeholder disappears as soon as you type, so it should never carry anything you need to remember. Some people also mistake hint text for something already filled in. That argues for short hints, especially after the first message.

The pattern that holds across all of them: the opening hint can describe what the chat is for, but once a conversation is going, the hint is either neutral ("Send a message") or says "reply". None of them repeats the opening invitation mid-conversation.

## Proposed behaviour

| Chat state | Placeholder |
|---|---|
| Empty project chat | "Ask about this print or request a change…" (unchanged) |
| Empty filament chat | "Ask about this filament or request a change…" (unchanged) |
| After your first message | **"Reply…"** |
| Newest Agent message shows answer buttons (your screenshot) | **"Or type your own answer…"** |
| Agent is still writing | "Agent is responding…" (unchanged) |
| A photo is attached and waiting to send | "add a note, or just send" (unchanged) |
| Printer panel | Its example answers ("e.g. 'bambu a1 mini'…") answer the panel's opening question, so after your first reply they go stale too. Switch to the same two rules above. |

I chose "Reply…" over "Reply to the Agent…" because the panel can be narrow and the shorter text never gets cut off. The answer-button hint tells you the buttons aren't your only choice, which is the one thing you can't tell from the screen today.

## Implementation size

This is small. The hint is chosen in one place, [Composer.tsx:240](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/components/Composer.tsx:240). The main app already computes whether you have sent a message ([App.tsx:605](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/App.tsx:605)), and the message list already knows when the newest reply shows answer buttons ([MessageList.tsx:287](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/components/MessageList.tsx:287)). The input box needs two more facts passed in, plus a visual test case for each new state.

- [Open WebUI MessageInput.svelte](https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui/blob/main/src/lib/components/chat/MessageInput.svelte)
- [LibreChat English strings](https://github.com/danny-avila/LibreChat/blob/main/client/src/locales/en/translation.json)

On 2026-10-21 Kenneth found 4 Release builds and 56 clang processes on 12 cores, all mine, in one worktree. Every ninja ran at its default -j (cores + 2), so 4 × 14 = 56. He pointed out that the orphaned processes were the smaller problem. The bigger one was that I put that many builds there at all.

What I did wrong, in order of weight:
1. I treated builds as free on a machine other sessions build on too. I never passed `-j`. I saw load 33, then 76, and started more builds anyway.
2. I restarted the build three times to change its target list or to slip in a small target. Each restart cost a full set of jobs. Waiting for the running build and adding targets afterwards cost nothing.
3. I went against the brief ("reuse the existing build; another session may be building") by configuring a fresh full-app build for an optional live check.
4. I blamed the slowness on "other sessions" without counting my own processes. That is the plausible-story-instead-of-checking failure from CLAUDE.md.
5. Mechanism: `pkill -f "cmake --build <dir>"` kills only the wrapper. Its `ninja -C <dir>` child keeps compiling as an orphan. I never checked that a stop had worked.

**Why:** the machine is shared. My extra jobs slow every other session, and two ninjas in one build dir can leave its records inconsistent.

**How to apply:**
- Before starting a build, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`. Cap jobs with `-- -j4` (fewer when load is above the core count).
- Decide the full target list once. Never restart a build to change it.
- Run one build per dir as its own process group (`set -m`, then kill with `kill -- -<pgid>`). After any stop, confirm with `pgrep -fl "ninja.*<dir>"`.
- Ask before a full-app build that the task did not require.

Related: [[background-bash-timeout-kills-builds]], [[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]], [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

**Why:** a nohup'd build survives the Bash tool timeout (see [[background-bash-timeout-kills-builds]]), so re-launching "the build" after each timeout adds a build instead of resuming one. ninja does not lock the build dir; concurrent instances just duplicate work and thrash.

- Never launch the same target set twice; wait on the saved PID with `kill -0` (see [[pgrep-wait-loop-matches-itself]]).
- Before ending a turn with the task done, kill builds you started that nobody will read (`pkill -P <ninja pid>; kill <ninja pid>`), or say in the recap that one is still running and why.
- To find who owns a stray build: the ninja's stdout path (`lsof -p <pid> -d 1`) contains the Claude Code session id; `ps -o args= -p $(pgrep -f -- "--resume=<id>")` shows the app session's side-session-notes path.

(function () {
  const log = (text) => fetch('http://127.0.0.1:18741/log?' + encodeURIComponent(text)).catch(() => {});
  let last = '';
  let step = 0;
  const type = (field, text) => {
    Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLTextAreaElement.prototype, 'value').set.call(field, text);
    field.dispatchEvent(new Event('input', { bubbles: true }));

  setInterval(() => {
    const field = document.querySelector('textarea[aria-label="Message the Agent"]');
    if (!field) return;
    const chips = [...document.querySelectorAll('.reply-chip')].map((chip) => chip.textContent);
    const bubbles = [...document.querySelectorAll('.message.assistant, .message.user')].map((m) => m.className.split(' ')[1] + ':' + m.textContent.trim().slice(0, 40));
    const now = `placeholder=${JSON.stringify(field.placeholder)} disabled=${field.disabled} chips=${JSON.stringify(chips)} messages=${JSON.stringify(bubbles)}`;
    if (now !== last) { last = now; log(now); }
    const ready = !field.disabled && !document.querySelector('.composer-stop');
    if (!ready) return;
    if (step === 0 && field.placeholder === 'Ask about this print or request a change…') {
      step = 1;
      type(field, 'my print failed');
      setTimeout(() => { document.querySelector('button[aria-label="Send message"]').click(); log('STEP sent first message'); }, 300);

      setTimeout(() => {
        [...document.querySelectorAll('.reply-chip')].find((chip) => chip.textContent === 'It stopped').click();
        log('STEP tapped "It stopped"');
      }, 1500);
    } else if (step === 2 && bubbles.some((b) => b.includes('Thanks, that helps.'))) {
      step = 3;
      setTimeout(() => log('DONE final placeholder=' + JSON.stringify(field.placeholder)), 1000);
    }
  }, 250);
})();

content.text:
The Agent chat's input box now changes its hint as the conversation goes on, and I confirmed it in the built app. The change is on `jusprin-newui` and not committed.

**What changed**

The hint is now chosen like this, in [Composer.tsx](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/components/Composer.tsx):

- **Empty chat:** "Ask about this print or request a change…" (the filament chat keeps its own wording). This stays even after the Agent's automatic note about an opened file, until you send something.
- **After your first message:** "Reply…".
- **While the newest Agent reply shows answer buttons:** "Or type your own answer…". It goes back to "Reply…" once the buttons go away.
- **Printer panel:** its "e.g." example answers stay until your first reply, then the same two rules apply.
- **Unchanged:** "Agent is responding…", the hint for an attached photo, and the text shown when the chat is disabled.

[App.tsx](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/App.tsx) works out whether you've sent a message and whether answer buttons are showing. The rule for when buttons show now lives in one function in [replyChoices.ts](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/replyChoices.ts), which both the message list and the input box use, so the two can't disagree.

**Tests**

- I added 10 visual test cases (project chat, filament chat and printer panel, each before and after the first message and with buttons showing) and one test where the hint changes over a live conversation. All 591 AgentUI tests pass.
- With the old hint code put back, 7 of the new tests fail: the ones whose expected hint changed. The other 4 cover hints this change keeps, so they pass either way.
- My first version broke one existing test. A reply that's still streaming could briefly show its answer buttons, which the old code prevented. I put that check back.

**Built app**

I ran the built RelWithDebInfo app with a scratch copy of its data folder, a fake API key, and a small local server standing in for the model, so no real provider was called. The script opened a model file, sent "my print failed" and tapped the "It stopped" button. The hint went "Ask about this print or request a change…" → "Agent is responding…" → "Or type your own answer…" (buttons showing) → "Reply…". I rebuilt the page bundle after the last fix and repeated the run with the same result. The app, the stand-in server and the scratch data are all cleaned up.

The printer panel was covered only by the visual tests, not by a run in the built app.

I've told the [Input placeholder design](#local_43f1d303-3345-4d67-8e2c-f87256cc1808) session that this is done.
Commit the placeholder change to jusprin-newui.
